meta.title: Who really said "Nothing is more common than the wish to be remarkable"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Shakespeare. It paraphrases Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., who wrote "Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable" in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Nothing is more common than the wish to be remarkable'?
meta.ogDescription: Shakespeare never wrote it. It is a paraphrase of Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.'s 1858 line, "Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable."

answer.label: Not Shakespeare — Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Holmes’s, but the popular wording is a paraphrase. In The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858) he actually wrote, “Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable.” The smoother “Nothing is more common than the wish to be remarkable” is a later rewording, and the frequent credit to William Shakespeare ↗ has no basis in his works.

source.heading: The real source

docMeta.dd: “Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable.”

source.excerpt: You long to “leap at a single bound into celebrity.” Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable. Fame usually comes to those who are thinking about something else,—very rarely to those who say to themselves, “Go to, now, let us be a celebrated individual!” The struggle for fame, as such, commonly ends in notoriety.
trail: The exact line appears in Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.’s The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table ↗: “Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable.”
Shakespeare Geek ↗ flagged the line as a Shakespeare misattribution and traced it back to Holmes.
Quote databases still split the credit: Goodreads ↗ files a variant under Shakespeare, while Quotefancy ↗ pins the paraphrased wording on Holmes.
source.excerptNote: From a letter Holmes reproduces in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, advising a young writer against chasing celebrity.

author.bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (1809–1894) was a Boston physician, Harvard anatomy professor, and one of the “Fireside Poets.” He is remembered for the witty, discursive essays collected as The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858) and for coining the term “Boston Brahmin.” He was the father of U.S. Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Shakespeare
misattribution.intro: This is a double error: the wrong author and the wrong words. The thought belongs to Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., but the wording most people quote is a paraphrase, and the name attached to it is usually Shakespeare’s.

items.tag: Not in any play, poem, or sonnet
items.why: The line is routinely credited to Shakespeare across quote sites — for example Goodreads ↗ — yet it appears in none of his works and has no early-modern source. It is a classic magnet-name misattribution.

items.who: “Nothing is more common than the wish to be remarkable”
items.why: Holmes actually wrote “Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable” in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table ↗. The circulating forms — “more common than the wish” and “so common as the wish” — both smooth away his original “common-place.”

misattribution.truthLine: The real author is Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., who wrote “Nothing is so common-place as to wish to be remarkable” in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table ↗ (1858) — not Shakespeare, and not in the smoothed wording usually quoted.

context.heading: What Holmes actually meant
lead: Holmes puts the line in a mock letter of advice to an ambitious young writer who longs to “leap at a single bound into celebrity.” His point is deflationary: wanting to be remarkable is the most ordinary thing in the world — it is the mark of the crowd, not the exception.

He goes on to argue that real fame “usually comes to those who are thinking about something else,” while the naked struggle for fame “commonly ends in notoriety.” The irony is sharp: the very wish that feels distinguishing is what makes one common-place.
context.pull: “Fame usually comes to those who are thinking about something else.”
